newsitem.title: FRANCE: Libyan envoy sees solution in dispute with France.
newsitem.headline: Libyan envoy sees solution in dispute with France.

text.p: Libya's envoy to France said on Tuesday the two countries were on the way to solving their dispute over the 1989 mid-air bombing of a French airliner, but French officials denied there had been any new development.

Ambassador Ali Abdussalem Treki told French businessmen Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and French President Jacques Chirac had exchanged letters on the dispute over the bombing of the UTA airliner over the Sahara desert which killed all 170 people on board.
France wants to bring six Libyans to trial over the bombing, including two secret agents and Gaddafi's brother-in-law Abdallah Senoussi.
"We are on the right path...There has been an exchange of letters between the two leaders," Treki said.
"I can assure you that there will always be a solution to overcome this problem and revive cooperation between France and LIbya," he said.

An aide to Chirac confirmed Gaddafi had written to the French president last March to offer cooperation. She denied Chirac had replied, and said Gaddafi's letter was passed on to anti-terrorist judge Jean-Louis Bruguiere who is investigating the UTA bombing.
Bruguiere visited Tripoli last July following Gaddafi's offer of cooperation but Libya has refused to hand over any suspects.

Treki made no mention of any new development in the separate dispute between Tripoli, the United States and Britain over the bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 in 1988.
Washington and London are seeking the handover of two Libyans suspected in that bombing.

The United Nations have slapped tough economic sanctions on Libya, including a ban on international air connections, in order to force Tripoli to cooperate in the probes on the bombing of the two airliners.

Treki was addressing French businessmen in a bid to boost investment and tourism in Libya. The ban on air travel to Libya currently forces visitors to sail to Tripoli, or fly to Tunisia or Egypt and go on overland.
